title: The six tapestries that helped a shareholders’ meeting room sound better
summary: Six late seventeenth-century Flemish tapestries made by Geraert Peemans from designs by David Teniers III reached Banco de España in 1934. The bank acquired them for the shareholders’ general meeting room at its Cibeles headquarters. They furnished a formal space and helped improve its acoustics. The example captures the argument of the bank’s release on its new textile catalogue: purchase records, an object’s physical characteristics and the architecture around it can explain an institutional decision more fully than an attribution or date alone.

The catalogue brings together several years of research under Antonio Sama and Yolanda Romero. It studies 98 of the 347 works in the textile holdings. The selected objects comprise 15 tapestries, 60 carpets, six ceremonial heraldic hangings and 17 contemporary textiles, spanning the seventeenth century to the present. That is the scope of the published selection. Its distribution across object types cannot simply be taken as the composition of all 347 pieces. The release describes artistic and technical study alongside work on how items were acquired or commissioned and how they served the bank’s changing spaces. In the linked catalogue, the account on printed page 18 records an asking price of 1,170,000 pesetas and a purchase price of 400,000. Its notes identify contemporary board and architectural records. These historical transaction amounts say nothing about the tapestries’ current value.

Carpets commissioned from the Royal Tapestry Factory for Cibeles provide a second connection between the building and its furnishings. The heraldic hangings offer another type of evidence: their designs trace changes in the identity the bank displayed during the twentieth century. The contemporary section, which includes work by Aurelia Muñoz, Teresa Lanceta, Patricia Esquivias and other artists, shows how established materials and techniques have been adapted. The release presents these works in a shared collection without suggesting that a modern work and a historic furnishing were acquired for the same reason.

The bank links the book to the exhibition El plano flexible. Both grew out of the same research, but they make different things accessible. The exhibition permits direct viewing by reservation in Madrid. The freely downloadable catalogue preserves documentation beyond the exhibition’s closing date. Together they extend a programme that previously published studies of the bank’s broader art holdings and of its clocks. This is a release about the history and public stewardship of property, with no figures for current market values, conservation expenditure or returns on the assets.

questions.question: What evidence connects the 1934 acquisition to the room’s acoustic problem?
questions.detail: The catalogue identifies board records, an architect’s brief and a negotiated price. To establish the relative importance of acoustics and representation, compare the cited meeting records, correspondence, room plans and purchase documents. The original commission evidence would distinguish a motive stated at the time from a function recognised in retrospect.

questions.question: How did the editors select the 98 works studied from the 347 held?
questions.detail: The release specifies the scope and composition of the selection but gives no sampling rule. Review the catalogue introduction and collection inventories for the role of provenance, condition, attribution or representativeness. That matters before drawing conclusions about the collecting priorities of the institution from the published works.

questions.question: What can the surviving heraldic hangings show about institutional change?
questions.detail: The release identifies an evolution in visual identity but does not establish its timing or the decision-makers involved. Compare dated designs, commissions and photographs of ceremonial settings with archival records. That would help separate redesigns reflecting a formal institutional decision from changes attributable to an individual commission or a different use of the room.

limitation: The press release describes a 635-page catalogue. The downloadable edition on the bank’s collection portal contains 473 PDF pages, including its colophon. The sources do not explain the difference.
